explanations.explanation: Yes, he does, and he says it right up front: "See what large letters I am using to write to you with my own hand!" (Galatians 6:11). Paul, the apostle who wrote this letter, wants them to notice it. I think he's saying this one is personal. When my stamp comes out in big, bold lines, I want somebody to notice too.

Actually, Paul does point it out. He says, "See what large letters I am using to write to you with my own hand!" (Galatians 6:11). So the text is clear that he wants them to notice the big letters. Nobody has to squint at this one, friend.

explanations.answer: Persecution for the cross of Christ
explanations.explanation: That's it. Paul says these people push circumcision "only" to avoid persecution for the cross of Christ (Galatians 6:12). They want to make a good impression outwardly, and the pressure lands on the Galatians. Persecution for the cross is the whole reason he gives.

explanations.answer: A heavy fine from the council
explanations.explanation: No fine shows up anywhere in this passage. Paul says they do this to avoid persecution for the cross of Christ (Galatians 6:12). No council and no paperwork, friend. Just trouble that comes from the cross.

Nothing about an inheritance in these verses. Paul says they push circumcision to avoid persecution for the cross of Christ (Galatians 6:12). That's the whole reason he gives. The text stays focused on the cross.

Paul says the opposite. He writes, "For the circumcised do not even keep the law themselves…" (Galatians 6:13). So the people pushing circumcision aren't keeping the law either. Still, he says they want you to be circumcised that they may boast in your flesh.

Right, because Paul says, "For the circumcised do not even keep the law themselves…" (Galatians 6:13). The ones pushing circumcision aren't keeping the law. They still want it done to the Galatians. Paul notices that, and now you do too.

Yes, flesh. Paul says they want the Galatians circumcised "…that they may boast in your flesh." (Galatians 6:13). The boasting is about what they can point to on the outside. I'd say that's a pretty empty trophy case.
Close to the neighborhood, but not the word. Paul says they want to "…boast in your flesh." (Galatians 6:13). He never says they boast in the Galatians' faith. The boast is about the outside, friend.

Not freedom, friend. Paul says they want the Galatians circumcised "…that they may boast in your flesh." (Galatians 6:13). Their boast is about the body, not about freedom. The word that fits is flesh.

The cross, yes. Paul says, "But as for me, may I never boast, except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ…" (Galatians 6:14). He puts all his boasting in one place. I'd like to say I'm that disciplined, but I once bragged about a cookie for a whole afternoon.

Not the law. Paul says, "…may I never boast, except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ…" (Galatians 6:14). The people pushing circumcision weren't even keeping the law (Galatians 6:13). So the cross is the only boast Paul keeps.

The temple doesn't come up here. Paul says he'll never boast "…except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ…" (Galatians 6:14). That's his one boast, and it's the cross. I'd say that's a lot of focus for one sentence.

explanations.answer: The world has been crucified to him and he to the world
explanations.explanation: That's the one. Paul says the cross is the thing "…through which the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world." (Galatians 6:14). It goes both ways. He doesn't explain it further in this verse, so I'll just let those words stand.

explanations.answer: The world has made peace with him and he with the world
explanations.explanation: Peace with the world isn't what he says. He says "…the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world." (Galatians 6:14). That's a far stronger picture than a handshake. Peace does show up a couple of verses later: "Peace and mercy to all who walk by this rule, even to the Israel of God." (Galatians 6:16).

explanations.answer: The world has forgotten him and he has forgotten the world
explanations.explanation: Forgetting isn't in the text, friend. Paul says, "…the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world." (Galatians 6:14). That's about the cross, not about anybody's memory. I'd say that line is a lot heavier than forgetting.

Paul doesn't give uncircumcision a prize either. He says, "For neither circumcision nor uncircumcision means anything." (Galatians 6:15). Neither side wins. What counts, he says, is "…a new creation."

Right, because Paul says, "For neither circumcision nor uncircumcision means anything." (Galatians 6:15). He doesn't crown one side over the other. Then he says what does count, and it's a new creation.

A new creation, yes. Paul says, "What counts is a new creation." (Galatians 6:15). Circumcision and uncircumcision both get set aside. I was pulled out of a junk drawer and given a bakery, so a new creation sounds good to me.

Not quite. Paul says what counts is "…a new creation." (Galatians 6:15). A moment earlier he pointed out that the circumcised don't even keep the law themselves (Galatians 6:13). So the law isn't where he lands.
Abraham doesn't come up in this passage. Paul says, "What counts is a new creation." (Galatians 6:15). That's his answer, plain and short. I'd say that's a pretty big answer for such a short line.
Peace and mercy, that's right. Paul writes, "Peace and mercy to all who walk by this rule…" (Galatians 6:16). It's a blessing for everyone who walks by it. Not a bad thing to have on a letter.

Wealth and long life aren't in this blessing. Paul says, "Peace and mercy to all who walk by this rule…" (Galatians 6:16). I think a blessing like that is worth more than a full cookie jar. Okay, a very full cookie jar.
Good words, but not the ones Paul wrote. He says, "Peace and mercy to all who walk by this rule…" (Galatians 6:16). So the blessing is peace and mercy. Simple as that, friend.

Yes, and he gives that reason in the same breath. Paul says, "From now on let no one cause me trouble, for I bear on my body the marks of Jesus." (Galatians 6:17). The text doesn't spell out what the marks are, so I won't guess. He just says he carries them.

Paul actually says it. He writes, "From now on let no one cause me trouble, for I bear on my body the marks of Jesus." (Galatians 6:17). The reason is right there in the verse. I'd say he's pretty clear.

explanations.answer: The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ
explanations.explanation: That's the one. Paul closes with, "The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit, brothers. Amen." (Galatians 6:18). It's a warm way to end a letter that had some hard words in it. I'd take that over a stern goodbye any day.

explanations.answer: The strength of our father Abraham
explanations.explanation: Not this time. Paul says, "The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit, brothers." (Galatians 6:18). Abraham isn't in this blessing at all. The grace comes from our Lord Jesus Christ.

explanations.answer: The wisdom of the prophets of old
explanations.explanation: The prophets don't show up in this blessing. Paul writes, "The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit, brothers." (Galatians 6:18). Grace is what he wants for them. That's how the letter ends.
